title: Efo Riro
author: Jemimah Ogunleye
desc: Bell pepper and scotch bonnet fried fifteen to twenty minutes until the pepper dries out and reduces by almost half — and no tomatoes, which the author calls an absolute rule.
longDesc: Efo riro means stirred leaf, and this is the version that defines itself by what it leaves out. The rule is stated flatly: using tomatoes for efo riro is an absolute no. What you get instead is a pepper base — tatashe and rodo blended coarse — fried hard for fifteen to twenty minutes until it has lost its water and reduced by half, so the finished soup tastes of pepper and palm oil rather than of stew. The greens go in raw at the very end and the pot comes off the heat.
ingredients: 2 bunches ugwu leaves (or spinach or soko)
Assorted meats of your choice — shaki, kpomo, cow leg, smoked turkey or beef
steps: Season the meats with sliced onions and boil on medium heat, tougher cuts first, then the softer ones.
Just before they are fully cooked, add the stockfish and boil until tender. Set aside and keep the stock.
Wash the vegetables thoroughly with hot water to remove dirt, avoiding prolonged soaking so the nutrients stay in. Slice or chop.
Blend the scotch bonnets, bell peppers and one onion coarsely — not smooth.
Heat the palm oil on medium 2 minutes.
Add the remaining onions and fry until fragrant.
Add the locust beans and fry 1 more minute to release the flavour.
Add the blended pepper and the two bouillon cubes. Fry 15 to 20 minutes, until the pepper dries out and reduces by almost half.
Add one cup of the stock, or water, and boil 2 to 3 minutes.
Add the assorted meats, prawns, crayfish, stockfish and catfish. Season, and cook 10 minutes further.
Add the washed vegetables and combine.
Take it off the heat and let it simmer 5 minutes on the residual heat.
chefTips: No tomatoes. The author's rule, as printed: 'A major rule is; using tomatoes for Efo Riro is an absolute No No!' For the opposing position from another named Nigerian authority, see NGA009.
Fifteen to twenty minutes on the pepper is not optional and it is longer than feels right. You are waiting for it to dry out and halve in volume.
Blend the peppers coarse. Smooth gives you a sauce; coarse gives you the texture efo riro is supposed to have.
Wash the greens in hot water but do not soak them. She is explicit that prolonged soaking strips the nutrients.
The greens go in raw at the end and the pot comes off the stove. Five minutes of residual heat is all they get.
Do not salt if you are using seasoned meat stock. Taste first — between the stock, two cubes and the crayfish there is a lot of salt already in play.

Ugwu is the author's choice, with spinach or soko permitted. The strictest reading of the dish uses shoko or tete; Yewande Komolafe glosses efo riro as 'Stewed Amaranth Greens', which points at tete specifically.
commonMistakes: Boiling the soup after the vegetables go in.
sources: Adapted from 'Efo Riro Recipe', byline Sisi Jemimah — quantities as printed: 2 bunches ugwu leaves, 3 medium or 2 big bell peppers, 1 1/2 scotch bonnet, 1/2 cup palm oil, 1 1/2 medium red onions, 1 tablespoon locust beans, 1/2 cup raw or cooked prawns (optional), 1/4 cup smoked prawns (optional), 2 Knorr cubes, 3 tablespoons ground crayfish, salt to taste. The 2-minute oil heat, the 1 minute on the iru, the 15-to-20-minute pepper fry, the 2-to-3-minute boil, the 10 minutes with the proteins and the 5-minute residual-heat finish are all hers.
The no-tomatoes rule is quoted verbatim from her page: 'A major rule is; using tomatoes for Efo Riro is an absolute No No!' Her ingredient list contains no tomato.
NOTE: the assorted meats, the dried stockfish and the smoked catfish carry NO quantities on the page. They are listed here as printed rather than estimated.

HEADLINE DISAGREEMENT, not reconciled. Tola Akerele, writing in Saveur, includes 5 medium plum tomatoes in her efo riro stew base (NGA009). Two named Nigerian authorities are flatly opposed on the single defining ingredient question for this dish. Both are published here.

Secondary disagreement on the greens: ugwu with spinach or soko permitted here; 2 1/4 lb shoko leaf named as the traditional one by Akerele; 500 g spinach plus 300 g collard greens by Abi Olayiwola, who flags that as a substitution (NGA010).
Secondary disagreement on handling the greens: added raw at the end here, with prolonged soaking warned against; blanched 6 minutes separately and squeezed dry by Akerele.
The Yoruba greens vocabulary is glossed clearly by Abi Olayiwola: soko is Nigerian spinach, tete is African spinach or callaloo, efo igbo is African eggplant leaves, ugwu is fluted pumpkin leaves.
reheating: Gentle heat. The greens are already at their limit, so warm rather than cook.
healthBenefits: Fluted pumpkin leaf is a strong source of iron, calcium and vitamins A and C.
Very low in carbohydrate for a main dish.
Red palm oil supplies carotenoids and vitamin E.
High in protein from the assorted meats, fish and prawns.
culturalNote: Efo riro translates as stirred leaf, and the name describes the action rather than the ingredients — which is why the argument about tomatoes is possible at all. It is one of the most widely cooked soups in Nigeria and among the most contested in detail, because the thing that makes it efo riro is a technique, and every household fills the technique with slightly different things.
